clue.text: Horseman heading off round lake? One won't break into a gallop!

definitions.text: One won't break into a gallop!

indicators.note: the shortened horseman's word goes round the lake's letter
the horseman's word loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: a horseman is a rider
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A rider ambles round a lake on a horse that refuses to gallop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' drops the R of RIDER to leave IDER, which then goes 'round' L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy, slow-moving person is the opposite of anyone who would break into a gallop.

clue.text: Agitated clientele setting a series of questions

indicators.note: agitated letters are stirred up, so the two words that follow are rearranged together

explanation.surface: Restless customers are being set a run of quiz questions.
explanation.walkthrough: All sixteen letters of 'clientele setting' are rearranged; the answer runs on into 5-down.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of examination is a set of questions designed to measure mental ability.

clue.text: Reluctant to accept Colin jiggling in such a garment

indicators.note: the word for reluctant takes in the rearranged name

parts.note: loth is an old spelling of loath, meaning reluctant

indicators.note: jiggling shakes the letters of the name into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates to accept Colin bouncing about in skimpy clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jiggling' rearranges the name to INCLO; LOTH is an old spelling of loath, still used in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cloth wrapped around the hips, a minimal garment of the kind the surface pictures.

clue.text: Olde-worlde beer served up — head of pint missing

indicators.note: missing tells us a letter is dropped from the turned beer
in a down clue, served up means the beer is written bottom to top

parts.note: porter is a dark beer

indicators.note: head of picks the first letter of pint

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned pub pours beer but forgets to top the pint with a head.
explanation.walkthrough: PORTER 'served up' (turned round, in a down clue) gives RETROP; the P, 'head of pint', goes 'missing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro styling deliberately imitates the past, as the mock-antique spelling Olde-worlde does.

clue.text: Supposed place resident initially abandoned

parts.note: to place something is to put it

indicators.note: the resident's word gives up its first letter

parts.note: a native is a resident of a place

explanation.surface: A supposed location whose local first left it.
explanation.definitionFit: A putative thing is generally assumed or reputed to be so, which is what supposed means.

clue.text: Ruling groups I encountered in 'Paradise Lost'

indicators.note: lost here means the letters have lost their order, so I and the poem's word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone meets governing bodies while reading Milton's 'Paradise Lost'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encountered in' only joins I to PARADISE; 'Lost' rearranges all nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Praesidia is the plural of praesidium, a permanent executive committee such as the one that ran the Soviet state.

clue.text: See 1
One coming across partygoers in terrace

indicators.note: in places the partygoers inside the abbreviation for terrace

parts.note: Ter. is the street-name abbreviation for Terrace
ravers are people out partying

explanation.surface: Someone crosses paths with revellers on a terrace.
explanation.walkthrough: Ter. is how British street names abbreviate Terrace, as in an address.
explanation.definitionFit: To traverse is to cross, so a person crossing a space is one who traverses.

clue.text: Favourite of Mussorgsky (Dvorak not right, quite wrong)

indicators.note: quite wrong says the remaining letters are put in a wrong order
not right removes R, the abbreviation for right, from the composer's name

explanation.surface: A note on one Russian composer's favourite, with a sideswipe at another composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not right' takes R out of DVORAK, leaving DVOAK, and 'quite wrong' rearranges it. Mussorgsky was a notorious heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian composer drank himself to an early death, so this spirit was his notorious favourite.

clue.text: Transmits Hardy novel…or someone else's?

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the two words are given a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Something sends out a Thomas Hardy novel, or perhaps a novel by another writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a noun after Hardy but is the anagram signal; the definition reads 'someone else's (novel)', here Laurence Sterne's.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne wrote this eighteenth-century comic book, so it is a novel by an author other than Hardy.

clue.text: Cocktail can lead to keen quizzical glance

parts.note: an old fashioned is a whiskey cocktail
can is slang for a toilet, as is loo

indicators.note: the lead to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A drink may provoke a sharp, puzzled stare.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 23-down. LOO is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase describes a disapproving or doubtful stare, the kind given to something odd.

clue.text: US city not entirely thwarted in sport

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles

indicators.note: not entirely means the last letter of the word for thwarted is dropped

parts.note: to be crossed is to be thwarted

explanation.surface: A US city partly frustrated in some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: La Crosse is also a city in Wisconsin, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a field game played with netted sticks, originating with Native Americans.

clue.text: Remember American comedy star's about to take leading part

indicators.note: the letters for about move to the front of the star's name

parts.note: Steve Carell is an American comic actor, star of The Office
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: An American comic is about to play the lead role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star's' is the star plus 'is'; the star is Steve Carell of the US version of The Office.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall something is to bring it back to mind, a plain synonym for remember.

clue.text: Puritan flattens fish

parts.note: to iron something is to flatten it
ides are freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A puritan presses some fish flat.
explanation.walkthrough: The ide is a European freshwater fish, also called the orfe.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironsides was the nickname of Cromwell's Puritan cavalry troopers, so one of them was a Puritan.

clue.text: Mostly dismiss anger about — say — attack on religion

indicators.note: mostly drops the last letter of the word for dismiss

parts.note: to sack is to dismiss
to rile is to anger

indicators.note: about turns the abbreviation for say round

parts.note: eg, for example, stands for say

explanation.surface: Firing someone and fuming about it, as it were, sounds like an assault on faith.
explanation.walkthrough: SACK 'Mostly' gives SAC; EG turned 'about' gives GE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrilege is the violation of something sacred, an offence against religion.

clue.text: Mountain rescue provider, pre-eminent, had to involve Swiss city

indicators.note: to involve means to take in, so the Swiss capital goes inside

parts.note: star as an adjective means leading or pre-eminent
Bern is the capital of Switzerland

explanation.surface: A top mountain rescuer had to work in a Swiss city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pre-eminent' looks like praise for the dog but supplies STAR; Bern is the Swiss capital.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed of large dog is famed for rescuing travellers lost in Alpine snow.

clue.text: Gangster dismissing excellent means of strangulation?

indicators.note: dismissing sends away the word for excellent from the gangster's name

parts.note: Scarface was the nickname of Al Capone and the title of gangster films
ace means excellent

explanation.surface: A mobster rejects an excellent way to throttle someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a neck garment is only whimsically a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A long woollen neck wrap could, in a pinch, be used to choke someone.

clue.text: What Roy piloted round Iran should be this

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the abbreviation for Iran
piloted means steered about, so the letters of what Roy are rearranged

parts.note: IR is the international abbreviation for Iran

explanation.surface: Whatever plane Roy flew around Iran ought to be fit to fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piloted' rearranges WHAT ROY, and that goes 'round' IR. The whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Any aircraft someone flies must be safe and fit to fly, which is the meaning here.

clue.text: Reduction of this in church recalled moral standpoint

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the turned church abbreviation
recalled means called back, so the church letters are read backwards

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: a reduction of the word this cuts off its last letter

explanation.surface: A church withdrew some cutback, as a matter of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduction of' leaves THI; CE 'recalled' gives EC, and THI goes 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a moral principle or set of values that guides conduct.

clue.text: Extract from whales: a mass — cold mass — is about right

parts.note: M is the symbol for mass
a berg is an iceberg, a cold mass

explanation.surface: A whale product: a lump, an icy lump, is roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: IS goes 'about' R to make IRS.
explanation.definitionFit: This waxy substance forms in sperm whales' intestines and was prized in perfume-making.

clue.text: Corpse's beginning decaying contained by _____?

indicators.note: the beginning of the word corpse is its first letter

parts.note: food that is decaying has gone off
something contained by a box is in it

explanation.surface: Fill in the blank: what holds a rotting body?
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is the definition and the whole clue describes it: a C, then OFF, then IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A box for burial is exactly what a decaying corpse is contained in.

clue.text: Somerset town following much larger place

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in pages ff.
Rome is a city far bigger than any Somerset town

explanation.surface: A small English town trails behind a far bigger city.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a rural county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Frome is a market town in eastern Somerset, a straightforward place example.

clue.text: Mate getting nasty colic from vegetable

parts.note: bro, short for brother, is slang for a mate

indicators.note: nasty suggests the letters of colic are messed up

explanation.surface: A friend gets a bad stomach ache from eating greens.
explanation.definitionFit: This green brassica, related to cabbage, is a common vegetable.

clue.text: Given a suggestion, enjoyed music not books

indicators.note: not removes the letters for books from the clubbing word

parts.note: to have clubbed is to have gone dancing to music in nightclubs
B is short for book, so BB is books

explanation.surface: Someone took a hint and enjoyed the music, but not reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A solver who has been given a hint has been helped with a pointer, as a crossword helps.

clue.text: See 9
Run to rocks after attacked sailor drowned

indicators.note: after says the rearranged letters come after the other pieces

parts.note: to have gone for someone is to have attacked them
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: rocks means shakes up, so run to is rearranged

explanation.surface: A boat runs onto rocks after a sailor was attacked and drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocks' rearranges 'Run to' to URTON. The phrase is RAF slang from the Second World War for an airman killed, often lost at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang phrase means killed or lost, originally of airmen downed into the sea.

clue.text: Kissed, losing head, chasing sex, wearing finery

indicators.note: chasing means following, so the shortened kissing word comes after the other piece

parts.note: to bed someone is to have sex with them

indicators.note: losing head drops the first letter of the kissing word

parts.note: necked is slang for kissed

explanation.surface: A romantic encounter in fancy dress, told in bursts.
explanation.walkthrough: NECKED 'losing head' is ECKED, 'chasing' BED.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedecked means decorated or adorned, as someone dressed up in fine clothes.

clue.text: Nymph that's unlikely to make you buy?

definitions.meaning: a tree spirit of Greek myth

definitions.text: that's unlikely to make you buy?
definitions.meaning: a flat, dull advertisement that won't sell anything

explanation.surface: A woodland spirit described as a hopeless salesperson.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer in two for the second definition: a dull commercial.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a wood nymph lived in trees; split differently it is a dull advert.
